newsitem.title: SWEDEN: High voting is not a sign of good democracy-study.
newsitem.headline: High voting is not a sign of good democracy-study.

text.p: Higher voter turnout during general elections is not necessarily a sign of a successful democracy, a new study by an international democracy watchdog showed on Wednesday.
The International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA) said voting figures in the 1990s dispelled the idea that high turnouts were seen only in established Western democracies.
Heading turnouts in a list of 163 nations were Malta, the Seychelles, Albania, and Uruguay, with over 90 percent of those eligible voting, followed by Angola, Indonesia and Iceland.
"A high voter turnout in a general election does not necessarily equate to a strong and robust democracy," IDEA researcher Andy Reynolds told a news conference.
"On the other hand, low turnout does not mean people are content with the system or that there is an inherent weakness in the political system."
Only three of the top 10 nations in the 1990s were Western European democracies, including Italy with 85.2 percent.
Britain ranked 44th with 75.4 percent turnout, Germany came 51st with 72.7 percent and Japan came 115th with 56.6 percent.
IDEA's secretary-general Bengt Save-Soderbergh said the study proved high turnout did not always mean a well-run democracy or that a multi-party democracy was stable.
"Albania had the third highest voter turnout during the 1990s (99 percent in 1991, 89 percent in 1992 and 1996)," Save-Soderbergh said in the report.
"But that country's government became quickly embroiled in trying to salvage a collapsing state, precipitated by the perceived illegitimacy of the incumbent politicians."
Voting rates were also not linked to poverty or literacy.
"If they were, then you could say to poor people or poor countries you have to put up with dictatorship," he said.
"Elections are not to be equalled to democracy but they are without doubt one very important and indispensable element."
At the bottom of the list came Mali, Djibouti, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Egypt, Guatemala and Colombia with less than 32 percent of their eligible populations voting in the 1990s.
The United States and Switzerland came 139th and 148th in the list respectively with voter turnout of 44.1 percent and 37.7 percent.

Reynolds said the low turnout in the U.S. was due to a combination of factors including an "unfriendly" voting system, problems with people getting on the voters' rolls, and complications with citizenship laws.
Switzerland's low turnout at general elections was seen as due to the high numbers at local and other elections.

Stockholm-based IDEA, which was set up in 1995 to promote and advance democracy, said its study was based on information from over 1,400 parliamentary and presidential elections from 171 countries between 1945 and 1997.
It found voter turnout had risen steadily around the world from 1945 when it averaged 61 percent to the 1980s when it reached 68 percent, but started slipping in the 1990s.
"In the 1990s, with the influx of a host of competitive elections in newly democratising states, the average for elections since 1990 has dipped back to 64 percent," IDEA said.
